Verify Now Blog > PCB Routing Guidelines for Ground, Power, and Signal Traces PCB Routing Guidelines for Ground, Power, and Signal Traces by: Mila Oct 22,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB routing PCB routing guidelines PCB trace routing PCB ground plane PCB signal integrity Poor PCB routing can lead to signal integrity issues, EMC failures, and power instability, even when component selection and schematic design are correct. These problems often stem from discontinuous return paths, improper trace routing, or insufficient consideration of electrical constraints. This article covers key PCB routing guidelines for ground planes, critical signals, and power traces, along with a practical routing workflow and common mistakes to help engineers improve design reliability and manufacturability. Understanding PCB Routing Priorities PCB routing should not follow a rigid sequence of routing signals first, power traces second, and ground connections last. For multilayer boards, the stackup and reference planes should be planned before routing begins. High-speed interfaces, sensitive analog circuits, and switching power supplies also require early consideration of critical signal paths and current return paths. In practice, the following approach provides a useful starting point. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and grounding strategy. Determine which layers will serve as reference planes, provide continuous reference paths for critical nets wherever possible, and establish a grounding strategy appropriate for the circuit. Step 2: Route critical nets first. These include high-speed differential signals, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and switching power supply loops with strict current-loop requirements. Such nets often have tighter constraints on routing length, return paths, impedance, or noise coupling. Step 3: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths, copper areas, and routing paths based on operating current, allowable voltage drop, temperature rise, and power integrity requirements. Step 4: Complete ordinary low-speed signal routing. Route signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O (GPIO) using the remaining routing space while meeting electrical and manufacturing requirements. This is a general guideline rather than a fixed sequence for every PCB. Routing priorities should be adjusted according to circuit topology, component placement, signal edge rates, power levels, and design constraints. For multilayer boards, planning continuous reference planes in advance is generally more important than simply routing all ground connections first. PCB Ground Plane and Return Path Design A ground plane provides a reference for signals and a return path for power and signal currents. Poor ground plane design can increase return-path inductance and loop area, potentially affecting signal integrity, power integrity, and EMC performance. Key Ground Plane Design Principles Prioritize reference plane continuity. For multilayer PCBs, a continuous ground plane should be used as the reference plane for high-speed and sensitive signals wherever possible. Avoid unnecessary ground plane cuts or slots beneath critical traces. Otherwise, return currents may be forced to detour, increasing loop area and the risk of electromagnetic radiation. Choose a grounding strategy based on the circuit. Digital, analog, and power circuits may have different noise and return-current requirements. However, physically separating DGND, AGND, and PGND and connecting them at a single point is not a universal requirement. In many mixed-signal designs, a continuous ground plane combined with careful component placement and current-path management can provide better noise performance. If separate ground regions or single-point connections are necessary, determine the connection strategy based on circuit topology and the component manufacturer's recommendations. Keep critical ground connections short. The ground terminals of decoupling capacitors, return terminals of power devices, and ground connections near interfaces should use low-inductance paths whenever possible. Properly placed ground vias can help reduce parasitic inductance. The number and placement of vias in high-frequency regions should be determined according to current paths, stackup structure, and EMC requirements. Common Ground Plane Design Mistakes For multilayer PCBs, using a continuous ground plane is generally preferable to relying on numerous narrow, manually routed ground traces. For single-layer and double-layer boards, copper pours, trace routing, and component placement should be coordinated to provide continuous, low-impedance return paths for critical nets wherever possible. Common mistakes include: Splitting the ground plane unnecessarily and forcing return currents to take longer paths. Routing critical high-speed signals across ground plane splits or slots. Placing decoupling capacitors too far from power pins or using long ground connections. Leaving unnecessary floating copper areas that introduce parasitic effects. Connecting different ground nets without a clear circuit-level justification. There is no single ground trace width that applies to every PCB. Ground traces carrying significant current should be sized according to current, copper thickness, allowable temperature rise, and voltage drop. For multilayer boards, a ground plane will often provide lower return-path impedance than narrow, manually routed ground traces. Common Failure Analysis Consider an industrial data acquisition board where ordinary signals were routed before the grounding arrangement was fully considered. Several traces fragmented the reference plane in the analog section, affecting the return paths of some sampling signals. During operation, the board exhibited fluctuating measurements and failed to meet the expected EMC performance. Troubleshooting should focus on ground plane continuity, signal return paths, analog and digital component placement, and power supply noise coupling rather than assuming that the routing sequence alone caused the failure. Corrective actions should address the actual failure mechanism and may include rerouting traces, restoring reference plane continuity, or optimizing component placement. Routing Critical Signals and Power Traces High-speed signals, sensitive analog signals, and power circuits have different design constraints. They should be routed according to their electrical characteristics rather than assigned priorities based solely on signal frequency or trace width. High-Speed Signals and Sensitive Analog Signals High-speed differential pairs , clock signals, DDR signals, RF signals, and sensitive analog nets such as ADC inputs often require their routing paths to be considered during the component placement stage. （High-Speed PCB Routing and Differential Pair Design） Control routing length and return paths. Critical nets should avoid unnecessary detours and vias while maintaining a continuous reference plane. Whether a high-speed trace is sufficiently short depends on factors such as signal rise time, propagation delay, and circuit requirements, not just clock frequency. Control impedance and timing. For high-speed interfaces such as USB and HDMI, target impedance, trace width, spacing, and other routing constraints should be determined according to interface specifications and the actual PCB stackup. Differential impedance cannot be determined by trace width alone; dielectric thickness, copper thickness, reference planes, and trace geometry also affect it. For DDR and other timing-sensitive parallel interfaces, length matching should follow the timing budget specified by the component manufacturer rather than applying the same length-matching requirement to every signal. Reduce crosstalk risk. The 3W rule can serve as an initial trace spacing guideline, but it does not guarantee that crosstalk will be eliminated. Actual spacing requirements also depend on parallel routing length, dielectric thickness, signal edge rate, and stackup structure. Signal integrity simulation or testing may be necessary for critical nets. Keep signals away from major noise sources. Sensitive analog traces should be routed away from switching nodes, high-current loops, and other noisy areas whenever possible. For high-speed signals, the need for additional clearance from the board edge or the use of ground via fences should be evaluated according to specific EMC requirements. Ordinary Low-Speed Signal Routing Signals such as buttons, indicator LEDs, and general-purpose I/O typically do not require the same level of impedance control as high-speed interfaces. However, they must still meet electrical and reliability requirements. During routing: Meet minimum trace width, spacing, and manufacturing requirements. Avoid unnecessary detours and densely packed parallel traces. Keep traces away from critical high-speed nets, sensitive analog areas, and high-current power loops. Evaluate crosstalk and EMC risks for low-speed interfaces with fast edge rates or connections to external cables. Ordinary low-speed signals can generally be routed more flexibly, but they should not be treated as nets that only need electrical connectivity. Power Traces and Power Loops Power routing must provide sufficient current-carrying capacity, control voltage drop and temperature rise, and maintain appropriate current paths for critical power circuits. Size traces according to actual requirements. Trace width should be determined by copper thickness, whether the trace is on an outer or inner layer, operating current, allowable temperature rise, and trace length. High-current nets also require evaluation of copper temperature rise, voltage drop, and current density at connection points. A fixed trace-width-to-current table alone is not sufficient to determine whether a design is safe. Minimize critical power loop areas. For switching regulators such as DC-DC converters, prioritize the layout of high-(di/dt) current loops. Keep relevant connections short and follow the IC manufacturer's recommended layout for input bypass capacitors, power devices, and other critical components. This helps reduce parasitic inductance and noise radiation. Control noise coupling. Switching nodes and high-current loops should be kept away from sensitive analog signals and other noise-sensitive nets whenever possible. Spacing between different power rails should be determined by voltage, current, switching noise, and insulation requirements rather than by a blanket rule that all power traces at different voltage levels must be separated. Use decoupling capacitors appropriately. Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to their corresponding power pins and connected to the power and reference planes through low-inductance paths. Capacitance, package size, and capacitor combinations should be selected according to component requirements and power integrity targets. Decoupling capacitors cannot compensate for poor power loop design. Power traces are not always better when made wider. Excessive trace width can consume routing space needed by critical nets. Similarly, inner-layer copper is not inherently worse than outer-layer routing for heat dissipation. The appropriate routing approach depends on current capacity, copper area, heat transfer paths, and stackup structure. A Practical PCB Routing Workflow After the stackup and component placement have been planned, the following workflow provides a useful starting point. The sequence should be adjusted to suit the constraints of each project. Step 1: Plan the stackup, reference planes, and board outline. Define the board outline, keep-out areas, connector positions, and layer functions. Establish the reference planes and grounding strategy for critical nets. Step 2: Complete critical component placement. Position high-speed interface ICs, crystals, ADCs, power ICs, and power devices with consideration for signal paths, power loops, thermal performance, and EMC requirements. Step 3: Route critical nets. Prioritize nets with strict timing, impedance, noise, or return-path constraints. These may include high-speed differential pairs, clock signals, sensitive analog signals, and critical switching power loops. Step 4: Route other power nets. Determine trace widths and routing paths according to current, voltage drop, and temperature rise requirements. Check decoupling capacitor placement and power return paths. Step 5: Complete ordinary signal routing. Route GPIO, buttons, indicator LEDs, and other general-purpose nets while meeting design rules and avoiding unnecessary interference with critical nets. Step 6: Review copper pours and grounding connections. Complete ground pours, check thermal relief connections and ground vias, verify reference plane continuity, and remove unnecessary floating copper. Ensure that copper pours do not compromise return paths for critical nets. Step 7: Run DRC and perform a design review. Check trace width, spacing, vias, impedance constraints, differential pairs, length matching, and manufacturability. For high-speed or high-power designs, perform signal integrity analysis, power integrity analysis, thermal analysis, or EMC validation as appropriate. Common PCB Routing Problems and How to Avoid Them Common Failure 1: Discontinuous Reference Planes Cause EMC Problems On a controller board, high-speed signals were routed across a split in the reference plane to avoid other nets. This increased the distance that return currents had to travel, and high-frequency radiation problems appeared during testing. Such failures should be investigated by examining the routing, reference planes, and test results. Possible corrective actions include rerouting the signals, restoring reference plane continuity, or rearranging components and other nets to reduce return-path discontinuities. Common Failure 2: Digital Noise Interferes with Sensitive Analog Signals An ADC circuit exhibited fluctuating readings. Investigation revealed that the analog input traces were routed close to digital signals and a switching power supply, creating potential noise coupling paths. Optimization should focus on the analog input routing, reference plane, front-end filtering, component placement, and power supply noise. Measurements should be used to confirm the dominant interference source. Only after identifying the failure mechanism should engineers adjust trace spacing, grounding, or filtering. （Common PCB Routing Mistakes and Design Rule Violations） Conclusion Effective PCB routing requires more than electrical connectivity and compliance with design rules. It also involves careful consideration of reference planes, return paths, signal integrity, power integrity, current-carrying capacity, and electromagnetic compatibility. Planning the stackup and critical nets in advance, applying routing strategies appropriate to each circuit, and performing a thorough design review can help reduce design defects, lower rework costs, and improve product reliability. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. However, pin names alone do not tell the whole story. Always check the IC datasheet to confirm each pin’s function and recommended connections. During PCB layout , pay particular attention to switching nodes, feedback paths, and grounding. Proper component placement and routing can help reduce noise, improve power integrity, and ensure stable operation. Whether you’re designing a simple power supply or a more complex DC-DC converter, understanding these pins is an important step toward reliable PCB design. Verify Now Blog > Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Reflow Soldering Wave Soldering SMT vs. THT PCB Assembly PCB Soldering As hardware engineers, we design the PCB, select the components, and send the Gerber files to the manufacturer. But have you ever wondered why some components go through reflow soldering while others require wave soldering? Both processes melt solder to form electrical and mechanical connections, so why does a production line need two different types of equipment? The reason is not that equipment manufacturers are making the process unnecessarily complicated. The main difference between reflow soldering and wave soldering lies in how the solder reaches the joints and which types of components each process is best suited for. For hardware engineers, understanding these two processes is more than just useful knowledge. It can affect PCB layout , component selection, pad design, and even troubleshooting during manufacturing. How Reflow Soldering Works Reflow soldering is primarily used for surface-mount technology (SMT) components, such as resistors, capacitors, SOPs, QFNs, and BGAs. The basic process is straightforward: solder paste is first printed onto the PCB pads, and the components are then placed on the board. Next, the PCB assembly passes through a reflow oven, where the solder paste goes through several stages, including preheating, heating, time above the liquidus temperature, and cooling. These stages allow the solder to melt, wet the surfaces, and solidify to form reliable joints. One detail that is easy to overlook is that reflow soldering is not simply about heating the entire PCB to a fixed temperature. The temperature profile over time must be carefully controlled. Taking the common SAC305 lead-free solder alloy as an example, its melting range is approximately 217–220°C. During reflow, the solder joint temperature must rise above the liquidus temperature and remain there for a certain period. However, the peak temperature, time above liquidus, and heating and cooling rates depend on factors such as the solder paste, component temperature limits, and PCB thermal mass. These parameters cannot be applied universally to every board. （reflow soldering） How Wave Soldering Works Imagine a PCB with small resistors, large connectors, and power pads connected to extensive copper areas. Small components generally have lower thermal mass and heat up quickly, while large components and pads absorb more heat and may heat up more slowly. If the temperature rises too quickly, the small components may approach their peak temperature before the solder on the larger pads has fully melted. On the other hand, increasing the peak temperature too much or extending the time at high temperatures to accommodate the larger pads can increase thermal stress on components, damage the PCB, and raise the risk of solder oxidation. The real challenge of reflow soldering is to ensure that every solder joint receives enough heat, but not excessive heat, while staying within the temperature limits of the components. （wave soldering） Why Reflow Temperature Control Matters Wave soldering works in a more straightforward way. The equipment melts the solder and uses a pump to create a stable wave of molten solder. After the PCB passes through flux application and preheating, its solder side comes into contact with the molten solder. The solder wets the component leads and PCB pads, forming the joints. Traditional wave soldering is most commonly used for through-hole technology (THT) components, such as through-hole connectors, transformers, relay sockets, and some power components. Their leads pass through holes in the PCB, allowing the molten solder to contact the leads and pads from the solder side and form reliable joints. Why Wave Soldering Isn't Suitable for Every PCB Wave soldering brings molten solder into direct contact with the solder side of the PCB. If the board contains a large number of surface-mount components, especially fine-pitch leads or packages with bottom-side pads, solder may bridge adjacent leads or cause soldering defects in components that are unsuitable for this process. However, this does not mean that surface-mount components can never be wave soldered. When wave soldering is used for suitable SMT components, the component orientation, pad spacing, and solder mask design must be considered carefully. In some cases, adhesive is also used to hold the components in place during soldering. PCB travel direction, protruding lead length, and component placement on the solder side must also be taken into account. If the design is unsuitable, even well-adjusted equipment parameters may not be enough to ensure consistent production quality. It is worth noting that reflow soldering is not limited to surface-mount components, nor is wave soldering restricted to through-hole components. Other processes, including selective wave soldering and pin-in-paste soldering (also known as intrusive reflow soldering), are used in actual manufacturing. Component and Pad Design For SMT packages such as QFNs and BGAs, engineers need to consider pad dimensions, solder paste printing, stencil design, and the reflow temperature profile. Package and pad design affect not only electrical performance but also soldering quality during PCB assembly. 2. Copper Distribution and Thermal Management When a power component's pad is connected to a large copper area, the copper can absorb and distribute heat, making it more difficult for the local pad to reach the required temperature. This may prevent the solder from melting sufficiently. During design, engineers should evaluate copper distribution, pad structure, and the actual temperature profile rather than simply increasing the oven temperature to compensate. 3. Hardware engineers do not necessarily need to operate soldering equipment themselves, but they should understand how their designs affect manufacturability. Reflow soldering focuses on controlling the temperature profile during solder paste melting, while wave soldering focuses on controlling the contact between molten solder and the PCB's solder side. Neither process is universally better than the other. The right choice depends on component packages, PCB layout, and production requirements. But have you ever wondered why some components go through reflow soldering while others require wave soldering? Both processes melt solder to form electrical and mechanical connections, so why does a production line need two different types of equipment? The reason is not that equipment manufacturers are making the process unnecessarily complicated. The main difference between reflow soldering and wave soldering lies in how the solder reaches the joints and which types of components each process is best suited for. For hardware engineers, understanding these two processes is more than just useful knowledge. It can affect PCB layout , component selection, pad design, and even troubleshooting during manufacturing. The basic process is straightforward: solder paste is first printed onto the PCB pads, and the components are then placed on the board. Next, the PCB assembly passes through a reflow oven, where the solder paste goes through several stages, including preheating, heating, time above the liquidus temperature, and cooling. These stages allow the solder to melt, wet the surfaces, and solidify to form reliable joints. One detail that is easy to overlook is that reflow soldering is not simply about heating the entire PCB to a fixed temperature. The temperature profile over time must be carefully controlled. Taking the common SAC305 lead-free solder alloy as an example, its melting range is approximately 217–220°C. During reflow, the solder joint temperature must rise above the liquidus temperature and remain there for a certain period. However, the peak temperature, time above liquidus, and heating and cooling rates depend on factors such as the solder paste, component temperature limits, and PCB thermal mass. These parameters cannot be applied universally to every board. （reflow soldering） How Wave Soldering Works Imagine a PCB with small resistors, large connectors, and power pads connected to extensive copper areas. Small components generally have lower thermal mass and heat up quickly, while large components and pads absorb more heat and may heat up more slowly. If the temperature rises too quickly, the small components may approach their peak temperature before the solder on the larger pads has fully melted. On the other hand, increasing the peak temperature too much or extending the time at high temperatures to accommodate the larger pads can increase thermal stress on components, damage the PCB, and raise the risk of solder oxidation. The real challenge of reflow soldering is to ensure that every solder joint receives enough heat, but not excessive heat, while staying within the temperature limits of the components. （wave soldering） Why Reflow Temperature Control Matters Wave soldering works in a more straightforward way. The equipment melts the solder and uses a pump to create a stable wave of molten solder. Their leads pass through holes in the PCB, allowing the molten solder to contact the leads and pads from the solder side and form reliable joints. If the board contains a large number of surface-mount components, especially fine-pitch leads or packages with bottom-side pads, solder may bridge adjacent leads or cause soldering defects in components that are unsuitable for this process. However, this does not mean that surface-mount components can never be wave soldered. When wave soldering is used for suitable SMT components, the component orientation, pad spacing, and solder mask design must be considered carefully. In some cases, adhesive is also used to hold the components in place during soldering. PCB travel direction, protruding lead length, and component placement on the solder side must also be taken into account. If the design is unsuitable, even well-adjusted equipment parameters may not be enough to ensure consistent production quality. It is worth noting that reflow soldering is not limited to surface-mount components, nor is wave soldering restricted to through-hole components. Industrial 1-Channel ESP32-S3 WiFi Relay Module PCB Layout Guidelines for Special Component Placement Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Begallie 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. BGAs (Ball Grid Arrays) are a type of IC package where the pins are placed in the form of solder balls. Compared to traditional packaging technologies such as DIP (Dual In-line Package) or QFP (Quad Flat Package), BGA employs a higher-density pin layout. With technological advancements, there is an increasing demand in PCB design for complex and small-sized chips. These chips enable higher integration and functionality within smaller spaces. Hence, there is a need for a packaging method that can accommodate these chips with higher I/O density while maintaining cost-effectiveness. BGA (Ball Grid Array) is precisely such a packaging method that meets these requirements. What is BGA Assembly? BGA assembly refers to the process of mounting a Ball Grid Array (BGA) onto a PCB using the reflow soldering technique. BGA is a surface-mounted component that utilizes an array of solder balls for electrical interconnection. As the circuit board passes through a solder reflow oven, these solder balls melt, forming electrical connections. Steps of BGA Assembly The BGA assembly process typically involves the following steps: PCB Preparation: The PCB is prepared by applying solder paste to the pads where the BGA will be mounted. The solder paste is a mixture of solder alloy particles and flux, which helps with the soldering process. Placement of BGAs: The BGAs, which consist of the integrated circuit chip with solder balls on the bottom, are placed onto the prepared PCB. This is typically done using automated pick-and-place machines or other assembly equipment. Reflow Soldering: The assembled PCB with the placed BGAs is then passed through a reflow oven. The reflow oven heats the PCB to a specific temperature that melts the solder paste, causing the solder balls of the BGAs to reflow and establish electrical connections with the PCB pads. Cooling and Inspection: After the solder reflow process, the PCB is cooled down to solidify the solder joints. It is then inspected for any defects, such as misalignment, shorts, or open connections. Automated optical inspection (AOI) or X-ray inspection may be used for this purpose. Secondary Processes: Depending on the specific requirements, additional processes such as cleaning, testing, and conformal coating may be performed after BGA assembly to ensure the reliability and quality of the finished product. Advantages of BGA Assembly Small footprint BGA packaging consists of the chip, interconnects, a thin substrate, and an encapsulation cover. There are few exposed components and the package has a minimal number of pins. The overall height of the chip on the PCB can be as low as 1.2 millimeters. Robustness BGA packaging is highly robust. Unlike QFP with a 20mil pitch, BGA does not have pins that can bend or break. Generally, BGA removal requires the use of a BGA rework station at high temperatures. Lower parasitic inductance and capacitance With short pins and low assembly height, BGA packaging exhibits low parasitic inductance and capacitance, resulting in excellent electrical performance. Increased storage space Compared to other packaging types, BGA packaging has only one-third of the volume and approximately 1.2 times the chip area. Memory and operational products using BGA packaging can achieve more than a 2.1-fold increase in storage capacity and operational speed. High stability Due to the direct extension of pins from the center of the chip in BGA packaging, the transmission paths for various signals are effectively shortened, reducing signal attenuation and improving response speed and anti-interference capabilities. This enhances the stability of the product. Good heat dissipation BGA offers excellent heat dissipation performance, with the chip temperature approaching the ambient temperature during operation. Convenient for rework The pins of BGA packaging are neatly arranged on the bottom, making it easy to locate damaged areas for removal. This facilitates the rework of BGA chips. Avoidance of wiring chaos BGA packaging allows for placing many power and ground pins in the center, with I/O pins positioned on the periphery. Pre-routing can be done on the BGA substrate, avoiding chaotic wiring of I/O pins. PCBWay BGA Assembly Capabilities PCBWay is a globally renowned manufacturer for PCB fabrication and PCB assembly. Types of Solder We offer both leaded and lead-free (RoHS Compliant) assembly services for our customers. Please choose one to best fit your PCB and the parts on the PCB. 5. Component Size Passive Component: we can accept components as small as 01005, 0201,0402. BGA: We have the ability to handle BGA of 0.25mm pitch with X-ray testing. Board Shape We can assemble boards in Rectangular, Circular and any Odd Shapes. SMT, which stands for Surface Mount Technology, is a method of directly mounting electronic components onto the surface of a PCB. This method is commonly used for installing Surface Mount Devices (SMDs), which have smaller pins or are pinless in structure. Compared to traditional through-hole technology, SMT provides higher levels of automated manufacturing capabilities, reduces costs, and improves quality. Additionally, SMT allows for the installation of more components on a limited PCB board area. Through-hole technology is typically used for components such as large transformers and high-power heat-dissipating semiconductors that are not suitable for surface mounting. SMT components have smaller leads or no leads at all, and common structures include short pins or leads, flat contacts, and Ball Grid Arrays (BGAs). PCBWay SMT Assembly Capability Overview We have the capabilities to assemble SMT prototype PCBs in small production runs with manual and/or automated SMT production processes, including single- or double-sided component insertions. Our production facilities can assemble the following SMT types: Ball Grid Array (BGA) Ultra-Fine Ball Grid Array (uBGA) Quad Flat Pack No-Lead (QFN) Quad Flat Package (QFP) Small Outline Integrated Circuit (SOIC) Plastic Leaded Chip Carrier (PLCC) Package-On-Package (PoP) Small Chip Packages (0.2mm pitch ) Main SMT Machines in PCBWay Automatic Solder Paste Printer Reflow Soldering Machine Pick & Place Machine Inspection equipment (3D SPI machine, online AOI machine, offline AOI machine, X-Ray machine) SMT Manufacturing Process SMT Process Flow Chart PCB, SMC, Stencil Preparation and Examination Prepare the PCB, surface-mount components, and stencil, and inspect them for any defects. Solder Paste Printing The solder paste screen printing machine used for SMT is required to print solder paste onto the PCB before surface-mount components undergo reflow soldering. 3D Solder Paste Inspection The solder paste printing process is one of the most critical stages in SMT assembly. The earlier the defects are identified, the lower the cost of correcting them. To ensure defect-free solder paste deposition in the required quantity, it is recommended to perform a comprehensive inspection of each printed PCB before commencing component placement. 3D solder paste inspection not only checks the coverage area and short circuits of the solder paste but also accurately measures the shape and volume of the solder deposits. On the other hand, 2D solder paste inspection cannot assess the volume or shape of the solder deposition. Pick & Place The SMT pick and place machine is one of the most crucial equipments in surface mount technology. It is also referred to as the pick-and-place robot. Prior to soldering, it picks up SMDs and places them onto the PCB. Reflow Soldering Reflow Oven: After the surface mount components are placed, the PCB is sent into the reflow oven. Preheat Zone: The first zone in the reflow oven is the preheat zone, where the temperature of the PCB and all components gradually increases simultaneously. The heating rate in this stage is 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches 140°C-160°C. Soaking Zone: The PCB remains at a temperature of 140°C-160°C for a soaking period of 60-90 seconds. Reflow Zone: The circuit board then enters a peak temperature zone where the temperature rises at a rate of 1.0°C-2.0°C per second until it reaches a peak of 210°C-230°C. This melts the solder in the solder paste, bonding the component leads to the solder pads on the PCB. The surface tension of the molten solder helps to hold the components in place. Cooling Zone: In the cooling zone, the heated PCB and components gradually cool down, allowing the solder joints to solidify and stabilize. The cooling process is critical for the formation of solder joints and securing the components. It helps ensure the reliability and mechanical strength of the solder joints. If the circuit board is double-sided, the printing, placement, and reflow process can be repeated using solder paste or adhesive to secure the components in place. AOI Machine Inspection After the soldering process, professional quality inspectors will perform AOI on the circuit boards to check for any defects before the products are stored in the warehouse. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Digital Light Processing (DLP) Overview Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview:What Is a DLP 3D Printer? How Do DLP 3D Printers Work? Digital Light Processing is a 3d printing process where a projector is used to cure photopolymer resin. Very similar to SLA where the only difference is that instead of a UV laser to cure the photopolymer resin, a safelight (light bulb) is used. Objects are created the same as SLA with the object being either pulled out of the resin which creates space for the uncured resin at the bottom of the container and to form the next layer of the object or down into the tank with the next layer being cured on the top. A diagram illustrated the DLP setup. Source: DruckWege.de Objects that are printed with Digital Light Processing have less visible layers versus other processes such as FDM/FFF. Compared with SLA, DLP can have faster build speeds due to a single layer being created in one singular digital image whereas with SLA, the UV laser has to scan the vat with a single point (trace out the object layer). Also, the same photopolymer resins that can be used with SLA, can be used for DLP 3D Printing. Objects printed with this process have the same strengths and weaknesses. Similar to SLA, DLP is commonly used to generate highly detailed artwork, non-functional prototypes, and can be used to make molds in investment casting applications. Main DLP 3D Printing Technologies Digital Light Processing provides excellent capabilities for 3D printing / Additive Manufacturing processes with an eye on efficiency. DLP is your go-to method when opting for a quick printing process without compromising on the quality of intricate parts. Just like their SLA counterparts, desktop DLP 3D printers are built around a resin tank with transparent bottom and a build platform that descends into a resin tank to create parts upside down, layer by layer. The difference is the light source. DLP 3D printers use a digital projector screen to flash an image of a layer across the entire platform, curing all points simultaneously.Now that you know how SLA works, it’s time to take a closer look at DLP. DLP is a “sister technology” to SLA as the only big difference is the light source used to cure the resin. As we just mentioned, SLA printers use lasers combined with galvanometers to cure resin. With a DLP 3D printer, the light source is a specially developed digital light projector screen. Thanks to this screen, DLP is generally considered to be faster than SLA, and here’s why: With SLA, the laser has to individually cure the resin in a “point to point” technique. On the other hand, a DLP projector screen flashes an image of a layer all at once! Thus all points of a layer can be cured simultaneously. In this way, the print speed is increased in comparison to SLA since it takes less time to cure a single layer. Since the DLP is a digital technology, the 2D image that is projected is composed of pixels. When translated into three dimensions, they become voxels. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Digital Light Processing (DLP) Overview Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview:What Is a DLP 3D Printer? How Do DLP 3D Printers Work? Digital Light Processing is a 3d printing process where a projector is used to cure photopolymer resin. Very similar to SLA where the only difference is that instead of a UV laser to cure the photopolymer resin, a safelight (light bulb) is used. Objects are created the same as SLA with the object being either pulled out of the resin which creates space for the uncured resin at the bottom of the container and to form the next layer of the object or down into the tank with the next layer being cured on the top. A diagram illustrated the DLP setup. Source: DruckWege.de Objects that are printed with Digital Light Processing have less visible layers versus other processes such as FDM/FFF. Compared with SLA, DLP can have faster build speeds due to a single layer being created in one singular digital image whereas with SLA, the UV laser has to scan the vat with a single point (trace out the object layer). Also, the same photopolymer resins that can be used with SLA, can be used for DLP 3D Printing. Objects printed with this process have the same strengths and weaknesses. Similar to SLA, DLP is commonly used to generate highly detailed artwork, non-functional prototypes, and can be used to make molds in investment casting applications. Main DLP 3D Printing Technologies Digital Light Processing provides excellent capabilities for 3D printing / Additive Manufacturing processes with an eye on efficiency. DLP is your go-to method when opting for a quick printing process without compromising on the quality of intricate parts. Just like their SLA counterparts, desktop DLP 3D printers are built around a resin tank with transparent bottom and a build platform that descends into a resin tank to create parts upside down, layer by layer. The difference is the light source. DLP 3D printers use a digital projector screen to flash an image of a layer across the entire platform, curing all points simultaneously.Now that you know how SLA works, it’s time to take a closer look at DLP. DLP is a “sister technology” to SLA as the only big difference is the light source used to cure the resin. As we just mentioned, SLA printers use lasers combined with galvanometers to cure resin. With a DLP 3D printer, the light source is a specially developed digital light projector screen. Thanks to this screen, DLP is generally considered to be faster than SLA, and here’s why: With SLA, the laser has to individually cure the resin in a “point to point” technique. On the other hand, a DLP projector screen flashes an image of a layer all at once! Thus all points of a layer can be cured simultaneously. In this way, the print speed is increased in comparison to SLA since it takes less time to cure a single layer. Since the DLP is a digital technology, the 2D image that is projected is composed of pixels. When translated into three dimensions, they become voxels. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) Overview Features Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview: How FDM 3D printing works? The Basics Of FDM 3D Printing Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a 3D printing technology widely known for its speed, accuracy, and competitive cost. An FDM machine precisely extrudes melted plastic filament to create a part. FDM parts can be made in as fast as one day. Benefits Of FDM 3D Printing Fused deposition modeling can build fully functional parts in standard plastics. However, they have anisotropy in the z-direction (vertical direction) and a step-structure on the surface. Fused deposition modeling works with standard materials, for instance, ABS/PA/PC. Therefore, parts have good mechanical properties and are durable over time. Parts can be post-processed as any plastic part produced with conventional manufacturing. Features of FDM 3D Printing Advantages Precision We use the most advanced industrial FDM 3D printers designed to meet tolerances of +/- 0.004” or +/- 0.002” per inch, whichever is greater. Strength FDM printed parts are available in a variety of high-performance plastics for applications that require resistance to the elements. Large Build FDM can produce FDM parts with large build volumes up to 600 x 500 x 500 mm Rapid Turnaround FDM parts do not require tooling which reduces the manufacturing lead time from weeks to days. Real Thermoplastics FDM has the highest variety of real engineered thermoplastics. Part Production FDM is capable of producing end-use parts on-demand, increasing throughput and helping you get to market faster. Drawbacks Surface Quality Extruding material layer-by-layer,the surface has layer lines and fine details cannot be realized Scale Effect The unit cost and lead time will not be reduced as much as casted or molded parts. Layer Adhesion Parts have an anisotropy in the z-direction (vertical direction), and properties are weaker than base materials. Fused Deposition Modeling 3D Printing Materials Fortus FDM Materials Available at PCBWay: ABS ABS is a common thermoplastic with good mechanical properties and excellent impact strength, superior to PLA but with less defined details. +10 PLA PLA (FDM) is used for low-cost, non-functional prototyping. Offers greater detail than ABS, but is more brittle. Unsuitable for high temperature applications. +66 ABS-GF ABS-GF is a glass fiber-reinforced ABS filament designed for FDM 3D printing. It offers improved strength, stiffness, heat resistance, and dimensional stability compared with standard ABS, while producing parts with a fine matte finish and minimal visible layer lines. It is suitable for both functional mechanical parts and decorative items. Stratasys ABS-ESD7 ABS-ESD7™ (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene-electrostatic dissipative) is an ABS thermoplastic with static dissipative properties for applications where a static charge can damage products, impair their performance or cause an explosion. ABS-ESD7 prevents a buildup of static electricity, so it will not produce a static shock or cause other materials like powders, dust and fine particles to stick to it. Ideal for electronic products with circuit boards and for the transportation and industrial equipment industries. Most widely used to create jigs and fixtures for the assembly of electronic components, but it is also useful for building functional prototypes of fuel storage and delivery products, as well as cases, enclosures and packaging. PLA-CF PLA-CF is a composite reinforcement material made by mixing carbon fiber powder into a traditional polylactic acid (PLA) plastic matrix. It is designed to retain the advantages of PLA for easy printing while significantly improving its mechanical properties. PC (Polycarbonate) PC offers accuracy, durability and stability, creating strong parts that withstand functional testing. PC-FR PC-FR is a flame-retardant polycarbonate filament engineered for high-performance 3D printing where safety, strength, and heat resistance matter. Tested to meet the UL 94-2023 V-0 standard, the top level of flame resistance for 3D printing filament, PC FR is designed to prevent or slow flame propagation with exceptional self-extinguishing properties. The Basics Of FDM 3D Printing Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is a 3D printing technology widely known for its speed, accuracy, and competitive cost. An FDM machine precisely extrudes melted plastic filament to create a part. FDM parts can be made in as fast as one day. Benefits Of FDM 3D Printing Fused deposition modeling can build fully functional parts in standard plastics. However, they have anisotropy in the z-direction (vertical direction) and a step-structure on the surface. Fused deposition modeling works with standard materials, for instance, ABS/PA/PC. Therefore, parts have good mechanical properties and are durable over time. Parts can be post-processed as any plastic part produced with conventional manufacturing. Features of FDM 3D Printing Advantages Precision We use the most advanced industrial FDM 3D printers designed to meet tolerances of +/- 0.004” or +/- 0.002” per inch, whichever is greater. Strength FDM printed parts are available in a variety of high-performance plastics for applications that require resistance to the elements. Large Build FDM can produce FDM parts with large build volumes up to 600 x 500 x 500 mm Rapid Turnaround FDM parts do not require tooling which reduces the manufacturing lead time from weeks to days. Real Thermoplastics FDM has the highest variety of real engineered thermoplastics. Part Production FDM is capable of producing end-use parts on-demand, increasing throughput and helping you get to market faster. Drawbacks Surface Quality Extruding material layer-by-layer,the surface has layer lines and fine details cannot be realized Scale Effect The unit cost and lead time will not be reduced as much as casted or molded parts. Overview: How Selective laser melting (SLM) works? What Is SLM? Selective laser melting, or SLM, is a type of metal additive manufacturing or 3D printing. Often, the terms SLM and direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) are used interchangeably. However, the two technologies differ slightly, in that SLM melts pure metals while DMLS fuses metal alloys. Main 3D Printing Technologies SLM is one of the most exciting 3D printing technologies available today and is utilized both for rapid prototyping and mass production. The range of metal alloys available is fairly extensive. The end result has properties equivalent to those manufactured via traditional manufacturing processes. SLM is very similar to SLS, and both processes are covered under the powder bed fusion umbrella. The major difference is the type of feedstock or powder it uses. While SLS uses mainly nylon (PA) polymer materials, SLM is specifically for metals. Nevertheless, the basic process is the same. As demonstrated in the image above, the laser sinters the powder together, layer-by-layer, until the model is complete. However, there is one big difference between SLM and SLS. Due to the constraints of the SLM process and the weight of the material, SLM requires support structures to be added to any overhanging features. This differs from SLS, where the surrounding powder material can provide enough support, allowing freeform shapes and features to be realized. Diagram showing how SLM 3D printing works. Source: Spilasers The Process in Depth An SLM machine has a chamber filled with metal powder. This metal powder is then spread across the substrate or build plate in very thin layers by a coater blade. A high power laser then fuses a 2D slice of the part by selectively melting the powdered material. The build plate then drops down by the height of one layer, and the coater spreads another layer of fresh powder finely across the surface. The process is repeated until you have the finished part. This whole process is performed in a controlled atmosphere inside the machine. Once the part is built, it can be removed from the machine. SLM parts need to be removed from the build plate, which is often done with a bandsaw. Then you need to remove the supports. As the support material is the same as the part material, this can be difficult and a time-consuming process. The surface finish of the sintered parts is rough and, depending on your requirements, may need some post-processing. It is also common to machine parts to achieve fine tolerances and finish fine features, surfaces, and holes. This is mostly due to the high cost of the equipment and the parts, as well as the post-processing requirements. Overview: How SLS 3D printing works? What is Selective Laser Sintering? Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) is an industrial 3D printing process ideal for manufacturing end-use parts. In SLS, a laser selectively sinters polymer powder particles, fusing them together and building a part layer-by-layer. SLS produces functional plastic parts with isotropic mechanical properties that can be used for detailed prototyping or end-use low-volume production. The Basics Of SLS 3D Printing Selective laser sintering (SLS) is an industrial 3D printing process that produces accurate prototypes and functional production parts in as fast as 1 day. Multiple nylon-based materials are available, which create highly durable final parts. A thin layer of plastic powder is selectively melted by a laser. The parts are built up layer by layer in the powder bed. A laser sintering machine will coat a layer of plastic powder onto a build platform, which is melted by a laser (or multiple lasers). The build platform will then be lowered and the next layer of plastic powder will be laid out on top. By repeating the process of laying out powder and melting where needed, the parts are built up in the powder bed. When the build finishes, the entire powder bed with the encapsulated parts is moved into a breakout station, where it is raised up, and parts are broken out of the bed. An initial brushing is manually administered to remove a majority of loose powder. Parts are then bead blasted to remove any of the remaining residual powder before ultimately reaching the finishing department. Features of SLS Advantages Durability Nylon is a durable material with great impact strength, medium flexibility, and high resistance to environmental factors. Rapid Turnaround Parts can typically be shipped in 3-4 days, allowing for faster design iterations and speed to market. Parts Production SLS is capable of producing end-use parts on-demand, increasing throughput. Complex Geometry Geometries can be built more easily due to the 3D printing process, adding complexity without additional cost. Scalability SLS can make a single part or component as easily as dozens of production pieces. Precision We use the latest generation of SLS technologies to meet tolerances of +/- 0.005” or +/- 0.002” per inch, whichever is greater. Drawbacks Material Limits Now SLS has only Nylon 12(white, black) & Glass-filled Nylon (PA 12 GF) material, but we can expect metal and fullcolor plastic material coming soon! Scale Effect The unit cost and lead time will not be reduced as much as casted or molded parts. Applications for Selective Laser Sintering Concept Models The speed and versatility of SLS lets product developers create physical snapshots of their designs through the iterative process. Rapid Prototyping SLS can be used to create fully-functional prototypes, complete with moving parts, as well as all-in-one assemblies. Direct Digital Manufacturing The high accuracy and consistency of SLS makes it an ideal way to build large quantities of discrete or customized parts. Using two-component polyurethanes and silicone molds, Vacuum Casting is known for its fast production of high-quality prototypes or end-use products. Get a quote Rapid Prototyping 3D Printing Vacuum Casting (VC) Overview Features Processes Materials Finishes Industries Reviews Resources Quote Now! Overview: How Vacuum Casting works? What Is Vacuum Casting? This is a casting process for elastomers which uses a vacuum to draw any liquid material into the mold. Vacuum casting is used when air entrapment is a problem with the mold. Additionally, the process can be used when there are intricate details and undercuts on the mold. Also, it is applied if the material used to make the mold is fiber or a reinforced wire. The process is sometimes called thermoforming because the manufacturing process involves rapid prototyping where the plastic sheets are preheated. The materials are preheated in an automated vacuum casting machine until they are soft and pliable. How Does Vacuum Casting Work? Plastic films and sand are sculpted over a pattern using heat, vibration and vacuum to form a mould in the shape of the component to be cast. Suction by vacuum is used to hold the mould in place until the molten metal has solidified. Have A High-Quality Master Model Cure Process Filling The Resin Final Cured Process Copyright: Open University Copyright: Open University Manufacture: 1.An alternative to “conventional” sand casting processes, with the advantage of a cleaner working environment. Suitable for either “jobbing”, or fully automated production, although ideally the foundry should be specifically designed for the process. 2.The foundry needs to be specially designed around this process, with special moulding boxes with integral cavities and vacuum lines to accompany moulds. The process is patented and licensed from Japan. Relatively few non-Japanese companies have adopted the process. 3.Uses dry, unbonded silica sand which requires little compaction and is almost fully reclaimable; a major economic advantage. 4.The ethylene vinyl acetate film is 50–100 µm thick and is heated to 100˚C; the temperature is judged by the loss in opacity of the film. After thermal softening the pattern must be uniformly coated, without wrinkles or tearing. 5.Patterns of cast aluminium are cheaper than for “bonded” sand moulding and last longer, since the sand does not come into contact with the pattern. 6.Gating systems should allow the cavity to be filled rapidly. Vents and risers must be located in such a way that the unfilled portion of the casting cavity is at atmospheric pressure, to allow the gases formed in the initial stages to escape to atmosphere. 7.Knock-out is easy, since removal of the vacuum allows the sand to flow out of the box. 8.When casting cast iron, or other similar medium to high melting point materials, the surge of hot air and mould gases released at knock-out produces a cloud of fine silica dust, which is a serious environmental health hazard. 9.Products that have been produced include manhole covers and tractor sprockets. Ideal applications for Vacuum Casting Pre-launch product testing Small series of housings and covers Concept models and prototypes Benefits Of Vacuum Casting The following are advantages of using vacuum casting on duplicating products. High Precision And Fine Detail To The Finished Product When you are using silicone as the mold to your products. It ensures that the final product has great attention to the details. The final product ends up looking like the original product. Every attention to detail is considered and taken into account. Even when the original product has the most complex geometry, the final product looks like the original. High Quality Of The Product The products made using the vacuum casting method are of high quality. Also, the use of resin allows you to choose the right material to be used in making of the final product. This allows you to have a wider choice of flexibility, hardness and rigidity you want in your products. Also, this has a great influence on the final appearance of the product since the material used plays a major role. Lowers The Production Costs Using the vacuum casting process to make the product is more economical. This is because the process uses silicon to make the molds. Silicone is affordable as compared to aluminum or steel and makes great final products. Moreover, the material allows you to make more products from the mold. This makes this process more cost effective as compared to the use of 3D printing. A Great Method When You Want To Meet A Deadline This method is fast, and it takes you less time to finish making the finish products. You can take seven to ten days to make around 50 functioning prototype parts. This method is amazing when you are making a lot of products. Additionally, it is great when you are working towards meeting a deadline. After thermal softening the pattern must be uniformly coated, without wrinkles or tearing. 5.Patterns of cast aluminium are cheaper than for “bonded” sand moulding and last longer, since the sand does not come into contact with the pattern. 6.Gating systems should allow the cavity to be filled rapidly. Vents and risers must be located in such a way that the unfilled portion of the casting cavity is at atmospheric pressure, to allow the gases formed in the initial stages to escape to atmosphere. 7.Knock-out is easy, since removal of the vacuum allows the sand to flow out of the box. 8.When casting cast iron, or other similar medium to high melting point materials, the surge of hot air and mould gases released at knock-out produces a cloud of fine silica dust, which is a serious environmental health hazard. 9.Products that have been produced include manhole covers and tractor sprockets. High Precision And Fine Detail To The Finished Product When you are using silicone as the mold to your products. It ensures that the final product has great attention to the details. The final product ends up looking like the original product. Every attention to detail is considered and taken into account. Even when the original product has the most complex geometry, the final product looks like the original. High Quality Of The Product The products made using the vacuum casting method are of high quality. Also, the use of resin allows you to choose the right material to be used in making of the final product. This allows you to have a wider choice of flexibility, hardness and rigidity you want in your products. Also, this has a great influence on the final appearance of the product since the material used plays a major role. Lowers The Production Costs Using the vacuum casting process to make the product is more economical. This is because the process uses silicon to make the molds. Silicone is affordable as compared to aluminum or steel and makes great final products. Moreover, the material allows you to make more products from the mold. This makes this process more cost effective as compared to the use of 3D printing. A Great Method When You Want To Meet A Deadline This method is fast, and it takes you less time to finish making the finish products.
